## Answer

According to Apple's fiscal 2024 Form 10-K (year ended September 28, 2024), **four** reported results for fiscal 2024 versus fiscal 2023 were unfavorably affected by the weakness of foreign currencies against the U.S. dollar:

| # | Affected result | Currency cited | What the 10-K says (MD&A, Item 7) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Greater China net sales** (down 8% to $66,952M) | **Renminbi** (named) | "Greater China net sales decreased during 2024 compared to 2023 due primarily to lower net sales of iPhone and iPad. The weakness in the renminbi relative to the U.S. dollar had an unfavorable year-over-year impact on Greater China net sales during 2024." (p. 22 of filing) |
| 2 | **Japan net sales** (up 3% to $25,052M) | **Yen** (named) | "Japan net sales increased during 2024 compared to 2023 due primarily to higher net sales of iPhone. The weakness in the yen relative to the U.S. dollar had an unfavorable year-over-year impact on Japan net sales during 2024." |
| 3 | **Rest of Asia Pacific net sales** (up 4% to $30,658M) | No single currency named | "Rest of Asia Pacific net sales increased during 2024 compared to 2023 due primarily to higher net sales of Services. The weakness of foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar had a net unfavorable year-over-year impact on Rest of Asia Pacific net sales during 2024." |
| 4 | **Products gross margin and Products gross margin percentage** (up to $109,633M / 37.2% from $108,803M / 36.5%) | No single currency named | "Products gross margin and Products gross margin percentage increased during 2024 compared to 2023 due to cost savings, partially offset by a different Products mix and the weakness in foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar." (Gross Margin, p. 24 of filing) |

### Notes on scope
- **Only the renminbi (Greater China) and the yen (Japan)** are individually named currencies. The Rest of Asia Pacific net sales and Products gross margin discussions refer generically to "foreign currencies."
- **Not affected/unaffected:** The Americas and Europe segment discussions attribute 2024 changes solely to product/Services sales with no currency drag, and the **Services gross margin** increase is attributed to higher Services net sales and mix — not currency. The iPhone, Mac, iPad, Wearables/Home/Accessories, and Services net sales discussions contain no currency attribution.
- **Context:** The two named currencies' drag on Greater China and Japan was partially offset by stronger U.S. dollar-based pricing/mix elsewhere, since both segments still grew in absolute terms. Item 7A (p. 27) separately notes that changes in exchange rates, "in particular a strengthening of the U.S. dollar, will negatively affect the Company's net sales and gross margins as expressed in U.S. dollars," and Risk Factors (p. 16) note that weakening foreign currencies adversely affect the U.S.-dollar value of foreign-currency-denominated sales and earnings.

I reviewed Apple Inc.'s fiscal 2025 Form 10-K (AAPL_2025_10K.pdf, FY ended September 27, 2025; filed October 31, 2025). Below are the developments in legal proceedings and government investigations that the filing pins to a specific day or month of calendar year 2025.

## Item 3. Legal Proceedings (10-K page 18)

**April 23, 2025 — EU Digital Markets Act, Article 5(4) Investigation (two actions that day)**
- The European Commission **fined Apple €500 million** and issued a **cease and desist order** requiring Apple to remove technical and commercial restrictions that prevent developers from steering users to alternative distribution channels outside the App Store. Apple has appealed the Article 5(4) decision.
- Also on April 23, 2025, the Commission issued **preliminary findings in the Article 6(4) Investigation** (whether Apple's new contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces violate the DMA). If the Commission makes a final adverse determination, it can issue a cease and desist order and may impose fines of **up to 10% of Apple's annual worldwide net sales**, plus additional fines for violating a cease and desist order. Apple says it complies and has continued revising its compliance plan.

**April 30, 2025 — Epic Games v. Apple (N.D. Cal.)**
- The California District Court found Apple **in violation of the 2021 Injunction** and enjoined it from imposing any commission or fee on purchases consumers make outside an app; from restricting, conditioning, limiting or prohibiting how developers guide consumers to purchases outside an app; and from otherwise interfering with a consumer's choice to proceed in or out of an app.
- The court **denied Apple's motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction** and **referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California** to determine whether criminal contempt proceedings are appropriate. Apple appealed to the Ninth Circuit; its request to stay the decision pending appeal was denied, and the Ninth Circuit agreed to hear the appeal on an expedited basis.

**October 2025 (post-fiscal-year-end) — Ninth Circuit oral argument in Epic**
- The Ninth Circuit heard expedited oral argument on Apple's appeal of the April 30, 2025 decision. (This is the only Item 3 event dated to a month rather than a day.)

**Fourth quarter of 2025 — "Other Legal Proceedings"**
- Apple settled certain ordinary-course legal matters and claims during fiscal Q4 2025 that, individually or in the aggregate, did not materially affect its financial condition or operating results. No specific settlement date is given.

## Item 1A. Risk Factors — company with which Apple has a commercial relationship

**September 2, 2025 — Google search distribution remedies (10-K page 14)**
- Apple earns revenue from **licensing arrangements with Google LLC** to offer Google search on Apple's platforms and apps; these arrangements are subject to government investigations and legal proceedings. Following the August 5, 2024 finding that Google violated U.S. antitrust laws, the **U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ordered certain remedies on September 2, 2025**.
- The order remains subject to further proceedings before the D.C. District Court (which may change the interpretation or application of remedies, or order new/changed remedies) and to appeal by both the DOJ and Google. A reversal on appeal could reinstate remedies initially proposed by the DOJ, such as prohibiting Google from offering Apple commercial terms for search distribution, which Apple says could materially affect its ability to earn revenue from such licensing arrangements.

## Note on what is *not* dated to 2025
Several other dates in Item 3 fall outside calendar 2025 and are background rather than 2025 developments: the DOJ/state antitrust lawsuit filed March 21, 2024; the Article 5(4) and Article 6(4) investigations opened March 25, 2024 and June 24, 2024; Epic's January 16, 2024 compliance plan and September 30, 2024 motion to vacate; and Google's August 5, 2024 liability finding. The European Commission State Aid Decision sequence (Note 7) is likewise 2016-2024, with the $10.2 billion net charge taken in Q4 2024. Separately, the filing references "beginning in the second quarter of 2025" for new U.S. tariffs and a Section 232 semiconductor investigation, but these are trade measures rather than the legal proceedings or government investigations asked about here.

I found Boeing's 2025 Form 10-K (`BA_2025_10K.pdf`, FY ended December 31, 2025). Here is what the filing reports.

## The 2025 IAM District 837 strike

**Employees:** approximately **3,200** employees at Boeing's **St. Louis area sites** (represented by IAM District 837).

**Duration:** **101 days**.

**Calendar dates** (given only in the MD&A "Overview," Item 7): the work stoppage was **initiated on August 4, 2025**, and **ended on November 13, 2025**, when IAM District 837 members "voted to ratify a new contract."

**Operational impact:** the strike "disrupted our St. Louis operations," impacting programs including **F/A-18, F-15, T-7A Red Hawk, MQ-25 and Weapons**.

**Notable context (Item 1A, Risk Factors):** like the 2024 IAM District 751 strike, the District 837 strike "occurred despite having in each case reached a tentative agreement with union leadership on the terms of the proposed contract and union leadership having recommended its members vote to ratify the proposed contract."

## The current collective bargaining agreement with District 837

From the "Information about our principal collective bargaining agreements" table in **Item 1, Human Capital** (PDF p. 4; printed p. 2):

| Union | % of Total Workforce | Major Agreement | Principal Location | Expiration Date |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| IAM (International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers) | 25% | **IAM District 837** | **Missouri** | **July 2030** |

So the "current agreement" is the newly ratified contract, located in Missouri, **expiring July 2030**.

## What each figure refers to (and what it does not)

- **The 101 days** is the **length of the 2025 work stoppage** — a historical duration of lost work at St. Louis, not the life of any contract.
- **The ~3,200 employees** is the **size of the bargaining unit/represented population** of District 837 at the St. Louis sites, i.e., the number of workers who went on strike.
- **The July 2030 date** is the **contract expiration date** of the agreement in force as of the filing (ratified November 13, 2025) — the term of the current CBA, not a duration of the strike.
- The **"25% of Total Workforce"** figure applies to **IAM as a whole** (across Districts 70, 751 and 837), not to District 837 alone; District 837's own share is the ~3,200 employees.
- **The August 4 and November 13, 2025 dates** appear only in the MD&A Overview; the Human Capital section and the labor risk factor state only the "101 days" without dates.

## Useful comparisons in the same filing

- **IAM District 751 (2024 strike):** over **30,000** Boeing manufacturing employees primarily in Washington state; **53 days**; initiated **September 13, 2024**, ended with a ratification vote on **November 4, 2024**; halted production of most commercial aircraft and certain BDS products. District 751's current agreement expires **September 2028** (Washington).
- **IAM District 70:** Kansas, expires **June 2027**.
- **SPEEA** (~16,000 employees, 11%): two contracts expiring **October 2026** — the next labor event flagged as a material risk.
- **Total unionized workforce:** approximately **72,000 employees, or 40% of the total workforce of approximately 182,000**, as of December 31, 2025, under 32 independent U.S. agreements with nine unions plus agreements with 18 international representative bodies.
- Boeing does **not** disclose a dollar figure for the financial impact of the District 837 strike; it describes the effects qualitatively (disrupted St. Louis operations, affected programs) and notes that future stoppages could materially affect its financial position, results of operations and cash flows.

## Summary of the amounts

**1. Allowance for credit losses / allowance for loan losses — $587 million (net decrease, Firm-wide)**

Note 1 (10-K p. 173) states the guidance "was adopted on January 1, 2023 under the modified retrospective method which resulted in a **net decrease to the allowance for credit losses of $587 million** and an increase to retained earnings of $446 million, after-tax, predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card." The MD&A repeats this: the allowance for credit losses "also reflected a reduction of $587 million as a result of the adoption of changes to the TDR accounting guidance on January 1, 2023" (p. 131). Note 13 (p. 256) gives the identical figures.

This $587 million measures the **pretax reduction in the credit-loss allowance** resulting from switching modified-troubled-borrower loans off the required discounted-cash-flow (asset-specific) approach to the Firm's elected non-DCF portfolio-based allowance approach (retained for collateral-dependent and nonaccrual risk-rated loans).

**2. Allowance for loan losses by loan portfolio segment (Note 13, p. 258; MD&A, p. 132)**

Line item "Cumulative effect of a change in accounting principle" in the allowance for loan losses rollforward:

| Portfolio | Impact ($ millions) |
|---|---|
| Consumer, excluding credit card | (489) |
| Credit card | (100) |
| Wholesale | +2 |
| **Total (Firm)** | **(587)** |

These are the January 1, 2023 cumulative-effect reductions (with a small $2 million increase for wholesale) to each portfolio's allowance for loan losses. The **allowance for lending-related commitments was not affected** (shown as "NA"), and the investment-securities allowance was not affected by this guidance. Note that the 10-K provides this breakdown by **loan portfolio segment** only — it gives no allocation by reportable business segment (CCB, CIB, CB, AWM).

**3. Retained earnings — $446 million (increase, after-tax)**

Note 1 and Note 13: the adoption resulted in "an increase to retained earnings of $446 million, after-tax." This measures the **after-tax cumulative-effect adjustment to retained earnings** recognized at January 1, 2023 under the modified retrospective method — i.e., the net-income effect of the $587 million pretax allowance release (implying roughly $141 million of tax at the Firm's ~24% rate).

**One reconciling item to be aware of:** the Consolidated statements of changes in stockholders' equity (p. 169) show retained earnings "Cumulative effect of change in accounting principles" of **$449 million** for 2023. That total is *not* the TDR effect alone; it combines the $446 million TDR after-tax amount with roughly $3 million from the separate January 1, 2023 adoption of the fair value hedging portfolio layer method guidance (Note 1, p. 173; the HTM-to-AFS transfer also produced a cumulative-effect adjustment to retained earnings related to the investment-securities allowance, per Note 10, p. 230).

## Fiscal 2024 amounts (NVIDIA FY2024 Form 10-K, year ended Jan 28, 2024)

**1. Total provisions — $2.2 billion** (MD&A, Item 7, "Gross Profit and Gross Margin," p. 40):
> "Provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations totaled $2.2 billion for both fiscal years 2024 and 2023."

This $2.2 billion is the combined fiscal 2024 charge to cost of revenue and is broken into two disclosed parts in the notes:

**2. Inventory write-down (excess/obsolete inventory) — $774 million** (Note 10, "Balance Sheet Components," footnote (1) to Inventories, p. 68):
> "In fiscal years 2024 and 2023, we recorded an inventory provision of $774 million and $1.0 billion, respectively, in cost of revenue."

This is the write-down of inventory to the lower of cost or net realizable value for excess or obsolete inventory (excess quantities of products/components relative to assumptions about future demand and market conditions).

**3. Excess inventory purchase obligations — approximately $1.4 billion** (Note 10, "Balance Sheet Components," footnote (1) to "Excess inventory purchase obligations" within Accrued and Other Current Liabilities, p. 70):
> "In fiscal years 2024 and 2023, we recorded an expense of approximately $1.4 billion and $1.1 billion, respectively, in cost of revenue for inventory purchase obligations in excess of our current demand projections, supplier charges and for penalties related to cancellations and underutilization."

This is the charge for non-cancellable purchase commitments with suppliers for quantities exceeding NVIDIA's future demand forecasts (supplier charges and cancellation/underutilization penalties). Note that $774 million + ~$1.4 billion ≈ the $2.2 billion aggregate.

**4. Provision release — $540 million** (MD&A, "Gross Profit and Gross Margin," p. 40):
> "Sales of previously reserved inventory or settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations resulted in a provision release of $540 million and $137 million for fiscal years 2024 and 2023, respectively."

This is the credit to cost of revenue from selling inventory previously written down and from settling excess inventory purchase obligations.

**Summary table (fiscal 2024):**

| Item | FY2024 amount |
|---|---|
| Total inventory + excess purchase obligation provisions (cost of revenue) | $2.2 billion |
| — of which: excess/obsolete inventory write-down | $774 million |
| — of which: excess inventory purchase obligations (supplier charges, cancellation/underutilization penalties) | ~$1.4 billion |
| Provision release (sales of previously reserved inventory / settlements of excess purchase obligations) | $540 million credit |

The filing does not state a net dollar figure for the fiscal 2024 provision net of the release; that amount ($2.2 billion less $540 million ≈ $1.66 billion) is arithmetic on the disclosed amounts rather than a reported number.

**Supporting descriptions elsewhere in the filing:**
- Critical Accounting Estimates — Inventories (p. 37): NVIDIA "charges cost of sales for inventory provisions to write-down our inventory to the lower of cost or net realizable value or for obsolete or excess inventory, and for excess product purchase commitments," based on inventory levels and future purchase commitments versus assumptions about future demand and market conditions.
- Note 1, Inventories policy (p. 58): "We record a liability for noncancelable purchase commitments with suppliers for quantities in excess of our future demand forecasts consistent with our valuation of obsolete or excess inventory."
- PwC's Critical Audit Matter, "Valuation of Inventories – Provisions for Excess or Obsolete Inventories and Excess Product Purchase Commitments" (p. 49), describes this area as one involving significant management judgment over future demand and market conditions.

Per your instructions, the year-end outstanding balances (total inventories of $5,282 million; $1,655 million excess inventory purchase obligations in accrued liabilities; $16.1 billion of inventory purchase and long-term supply/capacity obligations), the 2.7% gross-margin impact, and all fiscal 2023 amounts are excluded above.

- **Measurement basis.** Impairments were measured as the excess of carrying value over fair value, determined using the income approach (multi-period excess earnings method, i.e., discounted cash flow), with the key assumptions being the amount and timing of projected net cash flows (including the expected impact of competitive, legal and regulatory forces), the probability of technical and regulatory success (PTRS), an asset-specific discount rate and the tax rate.

**Why the IPR&D balance is considered elevated risk.** The 10-K states that the assets most at risk of impairment are IPR&D (approximately $21.8 billion as of December 31, 2025) and newly acquired or recently impaired indefinite-lived brand assets, because such assets are recorded at fair value and then measured at the lower of fair value or carrying value at each reporting period, so even small declines in outlook after an acquisition or impairment can trigger a charge. **Effect on results.** Higher intangible asset impairment charges were cited as the first driver of the $503 million decline in 2025 income from continuing operations before taxes, and are excluded from Adjusted income as a "certain significant item" ($4,940 million in the GAAP-to-non-GAAP reconciliation).

**Context.** BCA deliveries (including intercompany) fell to **348 aircraft in 2024 from 528 in 2023** — 737: 265 (from 396); 747: 0 (from 1); 767: 18 (from 32); 777: 14 (from 26); 787: 51 (from 73) (p. 33).

**Count: five causes the filing ties directly to deliveries.**

**1. Post–Alaska Airlines 737-9 accident safety and quality actions, including the FAA's production constraints.** Following the January 5, 2024 door-plug accident, the FAA grounded and inspected the in-service 737-9 fleet, investigated Boeing's (and Spirit's) quality control system, increased oversight, and communicated it would not approve 737 production rate increases beyond 38 per month or additional production lines until Boeing complied with quality and safety standards. Boeing slowed production rates and delayed planned rate increases, and all 737-9s in production underwent enhanced inspection before delivery (pp. 24, 35–36, 6, 9). The 10-K states directly that commercial airplane cash outflows "reflect slowed and/or paused production and **lower deliveries** as a result of ongoing safety and quality improvement actions … following the Alaska Airlines accident" (pp. 42, 44).

**2. The IAM 751 work stoppage (September 13 – November 4, 2024).** The strike paused production of the 737, 767, 777 and 777X (plus the KC-46A and P-8 for BDS); production resumed in December 2024. The filing states: "The IAM 751 work stoppage **significantly reduced aircraft deliveries in the second half of 2024**" (p. 24), and lists the work stoppage alongside the accident and supply chain as a cause of "lower deliveries" (pp. 42, 44).

**3. Supply chain constraints and disruptions (with labor instability).** Boeing and its suppliers "are experiencing supply chain disruptions as a result of production quality issues, global supply chain constraints, and labor instability," which "reduced overall productivity" (p. 25); the cash-flow discussion again cites supply chain constraints as a driver of "lower deliveries" (pp. 42, 44). For the 767 this included "factory disruption, including supply chain delays and quality issues" (p. 36).

**4. Program-specific delivery constraints — the 787 business class seat delays and inventory rework.** "Delays associated with business class seats **adversely impacted 2024 deliveries** and will continue to impact deliveries in 2025," with roughly 25 aircraft in inventory requiring rework (p. 37). 787 output was also slowed to below 5 per month because of supply chain constraints and other production issues (p. 37).

**5. Certification/flight-test delays on new models and derivatives, plus the resulting inventory.** For the 777/777X, flight test delays and revised certification timelines pushed the first 777-9 delivery to 2026, the 777-8 Freighter to 2028, and the 777-8 passenger variant to no earlier than 2030, and the decision to slow the 777X rate ramp produced "further customer delivery delays" (pp. 36–37). It also notes ~55 737-8s built before 2023 (including ~40 for China customers) awaiting 2025 delivery (p. 36).

**What is deliberately excluded.** The filing gives several other explanations for 2024's weaker commercial results, but does not link them to deliveries: the $4,079 million of 777X/767 reach-forward losses; $443 million of 737-9 customer considerations (a revenue reduction); the higher R&D spend; $1,271 million of lower abnormal production costs; the cost effects of the new IAM 751 agreement and non-union pay enhancements; and the $6,562 million of BDS contract catch-up adjustments. Demand was not the issue — Boeing states it was "experiencing strong demand from our airline customers globally" (p. 25). The U.S.–China trade relationship is presented only as a forward-looking risk ("we may experience reduced deliveries"), not as a cause of 2024's shortfall (p. 11).

## Answer

**Source: Berkshire Hathaway 2024 Form 10-K (BRK_2024_10K.pdf), MD&A p. K‑43 and Note 26 "Business segment data," p. K‑109 (plus supporting disclosures in Note 20, "Income taxes").**

The filing gives essentially two stated reasons, one in the MD&A and one in the segment footnote, with the tax-credit/regulatory facts they rest on.

**1. It reflects how the energy businesses are actually managed and evaluated.**
In the MD&A section on BHE (p. K‑43), Berkshire states: *"The discussion of BHE's operating results that follows is based on after-tax earnings, reflecting how the energy businesses are managed and evaluated."* The segment table that follows is therefore presented on an after-tax basis ("net earnings attributable to BHE"), broken into U.S. utilities, natural gas pipelines, other energy businesses, real estate brokerage, and corporate interest and other.

**2. Income taxes are material at BHE — specifically because of production tax credits — and are intertwined with regulation.**
Note 26 explains the general rule and the exception: *"For most non-insurance businesses, pre-tax earnings are considered in allocating resources and capital, although income taxes are also considered at BHE, given the magnitude of production tax credits associated with wind-powered electricity generation investments and the related impacts from regulation."* In other words, pre-tax earnings are the normal lens for Berkshire's other non-insurance businesses because taxes are relatively routine; at BHE they are not, because the tax line is large and is shaped by regulation, so the chief operating decision maker (the Chairman/CEO and the Vice Chairmen) must consider taxes along with pre-tax results.

**Supporting facts the filing puts behind those reasons:**

- **The tax line is a huge benefit, not a routine charge.** BHE's summary shows pre-tax earnings of $2,292 million in 2024, $940 million in 2023 and $3,146 million in 2022, but an **income tax *benefit*** of $1,871 million, $2,022 million and $1,629 million respectively — i.e., **effective income tax rates of (81.6)%, (215.1)% and (51.8)%** — with the footnote noting the benefit *"includes significant production tax credits primarily from wind-powered electricity generation."* A pre-tax measure would therefore badly understate BHE's actual earnings (2023: $940 million pre-tax became $2,962 million after taxes), and would give no sense of the size or variability of the credit-driven benefit.
- **The credits are central to BHE's investment returns and are exposed to regulation.** BHE has invested roughly $7.3 billion in third-party sponsored wind projects through tax equity investments, and Note 20 states that U.S. income tax credits (a $2,575 million credit in the 2024 consolidated rate reconciliation) *"derive primarily from production tax credits associated with wind-energy generation of BHE and tax credits arising from affordable housing investments."* Because these credits depend on the tax law, regulation and the continued operation of qualifying wind assets, after-tax earnings are the measure that captures the real economics.
- **Taxes are a rate-setting input for BHE's regulated utilities.** The MD&A notes: *"The rates BHE's regulated businesses charge customers for energy and services are largely based on the costs of business operations, including income taxes and a return on capital, and are subject to regulatory approval. To the extent such costs are not allowed in the approved rates, operating results will be adversely affected."* Consistent with this, BHE's regulated businesses apply the authoritative guidance for regulated operations, deferring qualifying costs as regulatory assets and accruing certain income as regulatory liabilities (Note 1(t)), so the tax/regulatory interaction is embedded in the rate mechanism itself.
- **Consistency with the rest of the filing.** Berkshire's overall results-of-operations table (p. K‑33) presents all segments on an after-tax basis — e.g., *"After-tax earnings of our utilities and energy business increased $1.4 billion in 2024 compared to 2023"* — and the BHE commentary attributes 2024 utility improvement partly to *"income tax benefits from recognized wind production tax credits ($157 million)."*

In short: BHE is evaluated after income taxes because that is how the energy businesses are managed and evaluated, and because at BHE the income tax line is dominated by very large, regulation-sensitive production tax credits from wind generation (and because income taxes are themselves built into the regulated rate-setting process), making pre-tax earnings an incomplete and potentially misleading measure of BHE's results.

## Summary

Only **two** of the six companies state how much of the one-time TCJA transition (deemed repatriation) tax they still had to pay as of their FY2021 year-end, and only one states the total remaining amount.

### Apple Inc. (FY ended Sept 25, 2021) — $24.6 billion

In Item 7 (Liquidity and Capital Resources), under the heading "Deemed Repatriation Tax Payable":

> "As of September 25, 2021, the balance of the deemed repatriation tax payable imposed by the U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (the 'Act') was **$24.6 billion**, none of which is payable within 12 months."

This is the total remaining liability (not just the next 12 months). Note the offsetting balance-sheet item: "Long-term taxes payable" of $24,689 million, and the deferred tax liability for "Minimum tax on foreign earnings" of $4,318 million (separate GILTI item).

### Pfizer Inc. (FY ended Dec 31, 2021) — $8.3 billion

In Item 7 (Off-Balance Sheet Arrangements, Contractual, and Other Obligations):

> "Estimated future payments related to the TCJA repatriation tax liability that will occur after December 31, 2021 total **$8.3 billion**, of which an estimated $750 million is to be paid in the next twelve months and an estimated $7.6 billion is to be paid in periods thereafter."

Note 5A adds that Pfizer elected to pay its "initial estimated **$15 billion** repatriation tax liability on accumulated post-1986 foreign earnings over eight years through 2026," and that the third installment was paid by its April 15, 2021 due date, with the fourth due April 18, 2022.

### The other four do not disclose it

- **JPMorgan Chase** — No transition/deemed repatriation tax disclosure anywhere in the FY2021 10-K. Note 25 (Income Taxes) discusses only GILTI ("The Firm will recognize any U.S. income tax expense it may incur on global intangible low tax income as income tax expense in the period in which it is incurred") and its tax rate reconciliation shows no TCJA line for 2021 or 2020. Total income taxes payable of $5 million in Note 19/Note 13 is far too small to reflect a material transition tax.
- **Berkshire Hathaway** — Note 19 (Income Taxes) contains no transition tax disclosure; the tax note addresses only indefinite reinvestment of foreign earnings and unrecognized tax benefits.
- **ExxonMobil** — Note 19 (Income and Other Taxes) discloses only GILTI accounting and a $6.3 billion 2020 asset-impairment-related tax benefit; no transition tax or installment liability.
- **Boeing** — Note 4 (Income Taxes) references that "The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) one-time repatriation tax and Global Intangible Low Tax Income liabilities effectively taxed the undistributed earnings previously deferred from U.S. income taxes," but gives **no dollar amount** of the remaining transition tax obligation. Its contractual obligations table (Capital Resources) and Note 13 contain no transition tax line.

Of the amounts that **are** disclosed, the combined remaining transition tax is **$32.9 billion** ($24.6B Apple + $8.3B Pfizer).
